name: Interview market making, set 2
description: Interview market making: card updates, digit counts, Fermi, skew, arbitrage, linked contracts, a card option and a losing trade. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: Three cards are dealt face down from a full deck. A contract pays £1 for each heart among them. Before any card turns, you quote 0.6 at 0.9 around a fair value of 0.75. Then the first card turns over: a heart.
items.question: What is the fair value of the contract now, in pounds? Give four decimal places or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the heart you see, then value the two unseen cards from the 51 left.

byKey.old-deck: You gave each unseen card a 1/4 chance. One heart is gone, so each has 12/51.
byKey.no-update: That is the value before the reveal. One heart is now known.
byKey.add-one: You added the heart to the old 0.75. The 0.75 already counted that card, so keep only the two unseen ones.

explain.text: The heart shown is worth £1. Each of the two unseen cards is a heart with chance 12/51, as 12 hearts remain among 51 cards. So the fair value is 1 + 24/51 = 25/17 ≈ £1.47.

items.prose: The interviewer says: "Write out the whole numbers 1 to 200. Make me a market on how many times you write the digit 1."
items.question: What is the exact count?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the 1s in the units, the tens and the hundreds separately.

byKey.no-hundreds: You counted 1s in the units and tens only. Each of 100 to 199 also starts with a 1.
byKey.hundreds-only: You counted only the leading 1s of 100 to 199. The units and tens add 40 more.
byKey.from-100: You counted 100 to 199 but skipped 1 to 99, which hold 20 more.

explain.text: Units: one 1 in every ten numbers, 20 in all. Tens: 10 to 19 and 110 to 119, another 20. Hundreds: 100 to 199 add 100, so the count is 140.

items.prose: The interviewer asks: "How many black cabs, the taxis you hail in the street, work in London?"
items.question: Which order of magnitude would you give?

options.why: You allowed about one cab trip per person a year. Londoners and visitors take far more.
You gave each cab only two trips a day. A working cab does nearer 20.
That is one cab for every nine people in London. Most people never drive one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Estimate cab trips a year, then divide by the trips one cab can do.

explain.text: Say 9 million people take a cab once a month: 108 million trips a year. A cab does about 20 trips a day for 300 days, so 6,000 a year. That gives about 18,000 cabs, so the order is 10,000.

items.prose: You make a market in a contract, quoting 99 at 101 around a fair value of 100. Customers have bought 6 from you, so you are short 6. Your view of fair value has not changed.
items.question: How should you move your quotes?

options.text: Raise both the bid and the offer a little.
Lower both the bid and the offer a little.
options.why: You lowered both quotes. Lower quotes draw more buyers, so you sell more and get shorter.

options.text: Widen both sides and keep the centre at 100.
options.why: You widened the quote. That slows all trading but does not lean against your short.

options.text: Pull your bid and keep your offer where it is.
options.why: You pulled the bid, which stops the very trades that would cut your short.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which trades you want next: buys from customers or sales to them.

explain.text: Being short, you want customers to sell to you and not buy from you. A higher bid draws sellers and a higher offer deters buyers. So shift both quotes up, keeping the width.

items.prose: Three contracts settle on the same event. A is quoted 20 at 22 and B 30 at 33. Contract C pays exactly A plus B, and is quoted 56 at 59.
items.question: What profit can you lock in per set, in pounds, trading at these quotes?

widget.accept: £1: buy A at 22 and B at 33, sell C at 56.
widget.label: Profit per set in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price each way round at the side of the quote you would trade on.

byKey.offers: You compared C's offer, 59, with the offers on A and B. To sell C you get its bid, 56.
byKey.mids: You compared mid prices, 57.5 against 52.5. You trade at bids and offers, not mids.
byKey.bids: You compared C's bid with the bids on A and B. To buy A and B you pay their offers.

explain.text: Buy A and B at their offers for 22 + 33 = 55. Sell C at its bid of 56, and the payoffs cancel on every outcome. That locks in 56 − 55 = £1 a set.

items.prose: A contract pays the larger of two fair dice, minus 3, in pounds. A roll of 2 and 5 pays £2, and double 1s pay −£2. You quote a market 0.4 wide, centred on fair value.
items.question: What is your offer, in pounds? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the fair value first, then add half the width.

byKey.fair: That is the fair value. Your offer sits half the width, 0.2, above it.
byKey.one-die: You used one die's mean, 3.5. The larger of two dice averages 161/36 ≈ 4.47.
byKey.full-width: You added the whole width. The offer is half the width above the centre.
byKey.no-minus: You left out the minus 3. The contract pays the larger face less 3.

explain.text: The larger of two dice averages 161/36 ≈ 4.47, so the contract is worth 161/36 − 3 = 53/36 ≈ 1.47. A quote 0.4 wide puts the offer 0.2 above that. So you offer at about £1.67.

items.prose: One card is drawn from a full deck. An ace counts 1, a number card its number, and a jack, queen or king 10. A call struck at 6 pays the card's count minus 6 if that is positive, and nothing otherwise.
items.question: What is the fair value of the call, in pounds? Give four decimal places or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List what the call pays on each count, with its chance.

byKey.intrinsic: You priced the average card: 85/13 − 6 = 7/13. The call never pays below zero, so it is worth more.
byKey.court-ranks: You counted the jack, queen and king as 11, 12 and 13. Here each counts 10.
byKey.put: That is the 6-put, 15/13. The call is the put plus the mean less the strike: 15/13 + 7/13.

explain.text: The call pays 1, 2 or 3 on a 7, 8 or 9, each with chance 1/13. It pays 4 on a ten or a court card, with chance 4/13. So it is worth (1 + 2 + 3 + 16)/13 = 22/13 ≈ £1.69.

items.prose: You bought a contract at £96 that you valued at £100, within your size limit. It settled at £56, so you lost £40.
items.question: How should you judge the decision?

options.text: Sound, if the £100 value was well founded: one loss tells you little.
Poor, because it lost £40, which shows the £100 value was wrong.
options.why: You judged the decision by one outcome. A good bet still loses some of the time.

options.text: Sound, because a trade bought below its value cannot lose money.
options.why: You treated positive edge as a sure win. It means a positive average, and any single trade can still lose.

options.text: Poor, because you should have doubled the size after the loss.
options.why: You chased the last result by doubling after a loss. Size comes from the edge and your limits.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate the quality of the decision from the result of one trade.

explain.text: Judge a trade by its edge and size when you made it, not by one result. Buying at 96 against a value of 100 is a £4 edge. Check the value afterwards, but one £40 loss is not proof it was wrong.
